newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's 1997 gold demand seen rising by 10 pct-WGC.
newsitem.headline: China's 1997 gold demand seen rising by 10 pct-WGC.

text.p: Gold demand in China, one of the world's largest consumers, could surge by as much as 10 percent in 1997 to 246 tonnes, with the biggest increase coming from secondary cities, a World Gold Council (WGC) official says.

"If you look at China as a total, (demand) growth in some parts of the market has levelled and is rising in others, so if you balance it all, we are looking within a range of 10 percent growth in 1997," Emily Li, WGC's Hong Kong and South China manager, told Reuters in a recent interview.
China's gold demand in 1995 was 224 tonnes, unchanged from 1994, ranking it fourth highest in the world behind India, the United States and Japan, WGC figures show.
In comparison, the world's gold mines produced a total of 2,272 tonnes last year, Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd says.
Demand in China's largest cities had levelled off as an increasingly sophisticated range of consumer goods tempted affluent spenders away from investing in gold, Li said.
"Gold consumption in first tier markets like Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Shanghai has stabilised -- these people face more choices on investment vehicles," Li said.
Instead, smaller cities emerging as industrial centres where incomes were on the rise would provide the most important growth areas for gold demand in China next year, she said.
"Cities like Chengdu, Tianjin, Dalian, Shenyang and Wuhan are succeeding the major markets," Li said.
"Of course this has to balance with economic growth, incomes, government austerity programmes -- all that will affect consumption -- but you will see some of the secondary markets growing," she said.

China's gross domestic product in 1997 could reach 8,178 billion yuan ($985.3 billion), an increase of 10.5 percent compared with 9.6-9.7 percent this year, according to a report in the official China Daily last month.
The price of gold has wilted steadily this year to its current level of around $370 per ounce after a spectacular rise at the beginning of February to $415 per ounce.
Producer selling as mines hedge their output, combined with rumours of central bank gold sales, have depressed the price of a gold market supported only marginally by physical demand.
China's demand for gold in the third quarter of 1996 dropped six percent to 53.7 tonnes compared to the same period the year before, the WGC said in its latest report tracking gold demand.
The drop reflected slower economic growth, tighter credit and increased consumer caution which led to saving instead of spending on gold jewellery, the report said.
The WGC, backed by a number of producers, monitors gold demand in countries accounting for about 75 percent of gold consumption.
